---
title: "Tea, Caffeine & Decision Companion"
---

You tip hot water over a handful of leaves. Steam rises. The water darkens—maybe green-gold, maybe deep amber—and a smell fills the room that is somehow both sharp and soft. Twenty minutes later you are a little more awake. Sometimes you also feel a little calmer. Coffee can wake you up too. So why does *tea* so often feel like a different kind of alertness?

That question is the door into this site.

This is not a lab notebook and not a sales brochure. It is a short journey through a drink that almost everyone has tried and almost nobody fully explains. The facts come from owner-supplied source packs: chemistry that was checked, history that was dated, and psychology studies that were named. The owner of this site is an economist. We do **not** invent economic theories here. We only retell what those packs already support—in plain English a smart high-school student can follow.

## What this journey is about

Think of four chapters that follow one continuous thread.

First you meet the **leaf**—where tea comes from, why green and black look so different, and what hot water actually pulls into your mug. Then you follow those compounds **into the body**: how caffeine blocks a “time for sleep” signal, how L-theanine (a calming amino acid in tea) tends to support calm focus, and what researchers measure beyond “I feel better.” Next you zoom out. Tea remade **trade balances**, became a monastic focus aid, and even a warm mug in the hand shows up in experiments on trust. A short brewing break can also act as a practical stress reset. Finally you ask the decision question: do drinks **nudge** how fast we answer, how much risk we take, how much we care about tomorrow, and how trusting we are in a first move? Lab games measure those nudges—and the packs are honest about the limits.

You can start anywhere. But if you read in order, each chapter hands you a reason to open the next.

## The four chapters (at a glance)

1. **[The Chemical Core](modules/module-01.qmd)** — One plant species, two main types; processing that chooses green or black; brewing that decides what leaves the leaf; three headline characters in the cup: caffeine, L-theanine, and EGCG.
2. **[Body, Brain & Mood](modules/module-02.qmd)** — Why tea can feel “awake but not as jittery as coffee,” told through brain signaling, brain-wave patterns, stress hormones, and simple body signals.
3. **[History, Ritual & Warmth](modules/module-03.qmd)** — Empires and silver, monks and tea rooms, warm hands and trust, and the brewing sequence as a stress break.
4. **[Decisions & Choices](modules/module-04.qmd)** — Fast gut thinking versus careful thinking, risk and waiting for payoffs, trust games, and how careful studies are usually built.

A map of the whole trip sits on the [Modules overview](modules/index.qmd). Treat it like a travel itinerary: you can hop, or you can follow the route.

## How to travel with this site

When a number appears—say “about 30–50 mg caffeine”—treat it as a **typical range from the packs**, not a promise about your exact mug. Brands, leaves, and steep times differ. The [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd) is the quick table for a common 250 mL cup.

When a technical word appears, we define it in the story the first time. The [Glossary](glossary.qmd) is there when you want a one-line reminder.

When you wonder how a brewing fact connects to mood, or a warm mug to a trust game, open [Linkages](linkages.qmd). Those eleven bridges are the threads that sew the chapters together.

When you want the paper behind a name-and-year, use the [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd).

## What we refuse to invent

We do **not** invent new percentages, mechanisms, history figures, or study results. We do **not** paste walls of lab equations. Everything here should trace back to the verified packs or the bibliography list. That honesty is part of the story: curiosity without costume jewelry.

Ready? Pour an imaginary cup—and start with [Chapter 1: The Chemical Core](modules/module-01.qmd), or skim the [roadmap](modules/index.qmd) first.
